descriptions: not dependent on another, peaceful, not elaborated by elaborations, free of conceptual construction, without multiplicity — the mark of reality (MMK 18.9)
dependent origination, qualified by the eight negations, the pacification of elaborations, auspicious (MMK dedicatory verses)
the pacification of all apprehending, the pacification of elaboration, auspicious (MMK 25.24)
the emptiness which is dependent origination, which is a dependent designation and the middle way (MMK 24.18)
negations: no cessation, no arising, no annihilation, no permanence, no unity, no plurality, no coming, no going (dedication)
not arisen from self, other, both or no cause (MMK 1.1)
nirvāṇa is neither an existent nor a non-existent (MMK 25.4–10)
'empty' should not be said, nor 'not empty', nor both, nor neither — they are said only for designation (MMK 22.11)
emptiness is itself empty; it is not a view (MMK 13.8; 24.18)
relation_to_self: The self is not identical with the aggregates nor different from them (MMK 18.1; 27.4–8); it is a designation made in dependence on them, like a chariot on its parts (MA 6.150ff). Knowing reality is the ceasing of 'I' and 'mine' (MMK 18.2–4).
relation_to_world: Emptiness is not another thing behind the world: it is the world's being dependently arisen (MMK 24.18–19). The limit of nirvāṇa is the limit of saṃsāra (MMK 25.19–20). The world is accepted as conventional truth, and the ultimate is taught only by relying on it (MMK 24.10).
caveat: Madhyamaka rejects any reading of emptiness as a positive ultimate entity, ground, substance or absolute — it is the mere absence of own-nature in each thing and is itself empty; to take it as a view or a thing is called incurable (MMK 13.8). Calling emptiness 'the one truth named variously' would be admitted only as a conventional designation, not as naming a real referent. The school also rejects identification with the Upaniṣadic brahman or ātman (Madhyamakahṛdaya ch.8; Tattvasaṅgraha).

descriptions: the nature found by correct seeing, as against the nature found by false seeing, which is conventional truth (MA 6.23)
the reality which is not in the domain of the intellect; the intellect is said to be conventional (BCA 9.2)
the mere negation of own-nature, which implies nothing else in its place (non-implicative negation, prasajya-pratiṣedha)
negations: things arise neither from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without cause (Buddhapālita and Candrakīrti on MMK 1.1; MA 6.8–104)
the self is not found in any of the seven ways the chariot is sought (MA 6.151ff)
relation_to_self: Both the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of dharmas are emptiness; the view of a real self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the root of saṃsāra and is cut by seeing its object as unfindable (MA 6.120).
relation_to_world: The world is not negated as it is known by worldly people; it is accepted by worldly consensus (lokaprasiddhi), without analysis, as conventional truth, while under analysis nothing is found.
caveat: The name 'Prāsaṅgika' is a Tibetan classification. Candrakīrti and Śāntideva deny that emptiness is an entity or a thesis to be proved by autonomous inference; any 'one truth' reading as a positive absolute is rejected.

names.name: paramārtha (the ultimate), as object of the highest wisdom

descriptions: what is known by non-conceptual wisdom, beyond all elaboration (the non-nominal ultimate)
the negation of arising etc. established by reasoning, which accords with the ultimate (the nominal ultimate) (Madhyamakahṛdaya 3; Tarkajvālā)
that which is found by reasoning that does not deceive (Jñānagarbha, Satyadvayavibhaṅga)
negations: the earth-element etc. are ultimately not of the nature of the elements, because they are produced, like cognition (Bhāviveka's autonomous inference, Prajñāpradīpa)
no arising ultimately, from self or other (Prajñāpradīpa ch.1)
relation_to_self: The person is a designation on the aggregates; Bhāviveka identifies the conventional referent of 'I' with consciousness (mental consciousness) — a view Candrakīrti rejects.
relation_to_world: Conventionally things arise and function as they appear (the correct conventional); only ultimately are they unborn.
caveat: Emptiness is a negation, not an entity; the Svātantrika authors (who did not call themselves so) would reject treating it as a substantial ground.

names.name: niḥsvabhāvatā established by the absence of true unity and plurality
nirvikalpa-jñāna's object: freedom from all elaboration

descriptions: the absence of own-nature in all things, shown because nothing is truly one or truly many (MAL 1)
the ultimate is free from all elaborations; the nominal ultimate (the negation of arising) accords with it (MAL 70–72)
that which the yogin enters when analysing he finds no dharma arisen in the three times: non-conceptual wisdom pacifying all elaboration (Bhāvanākrama III)
negations: neither external objects nor mind are ultimately real (MAL 92–93)
relation_to_self: Persons and dharmas alike are without own-nature; conventionally there is only self-illuminating mind.
relation_to_world: The world of appearances is conventionally mind-only and 'satisfying only when not analysed'; ultimately it is empty.
caveat: Mind-only is accepted only conventionally, as a step; neither mind nor emptiness is posited as a positive ultimate entity.
